title: Friends of other beliefs
hookLine: give a reason for your hope with gentleness and respect (1 Peter 3:15), and listen as well
tomorrow: work shows up in Eden before anything goes wrong. so is work a curse?

lines: DO YOU ACTUALLY BELIEVE ALL THAT?
AN ALTAR FOR A GOD NOBODY NAMED.
cards: The concert's over, the car's warm, and the friend in the passenger seat finally asks it: okay, but do you actually believe all of that? Acts has a story that starts in the same spot.
Paul is in Athens, a city of temples and statues, and the people there want to hear what this new teaching is. So they bring him to speak.
But before he does, Acts says, he has been walking the streets, looking closely at what they honor. On one altar he found words carved for a god nobody could name. So where does he start?

teach.b: He starts with their altar. In the King James Bible: “For as I passed by, and beheld your devotions, I found an altar with this inscription, TO THE UNKNOWN GOD.” He looked before he spoke.
Then he quotes their poets, not his own: “For in him we live, and move, and have our being.”

And he tells them God “hath made of one blood all nations of men.” One blood: a single human family, named before any disagreement. Paul doesn't hide his own faith; he goes on to speak of Jesus and the resurrection.
Acts is honest about how it went. Some mocked, and others said, “We will hear thee again of this matter.” The door stayed open.

teach.h: SWIFT TO HEAR, READY TO ANSWER.
teach.b: The First Letter of Peter puts the posture in one line: “be ready always to give an answer to every man that asketh you a reason of the hope that is in you with meekness and fear.” Someone asks first.
The answer is about hope, not winning. The letter of James puts listening ahead of it all: “let every man be swift to hear, slow to speak, slow to wrath.”
And Colossians wants words “alway with grace, seasoned with salt”: kind, and still honest.
Gentleness and respect is that meekness and fear, in plainer English.

how: Christians talk about faith with friends of other beliefs in different ways; Paul's speech in Athens (Acts 17) and 1 Peter 3:15 are passages churches turn to for how to do it; churches take part in interfaith friendship and shared service in their own ways.

games.q: what does “friends of other beliefs” mean?
o: people you meet once and never see again
people you love whose answers to faith differ
people who share every belief you hold

games.q: Athens and after — tap the pairs.
p: in him we live, and move
swift to hear, slow to speak

s: Paul in Athens opened by condemning everything he saw
he opened with their own altar, and quoted their own poets.
in Acts, everyone in Athens either agreed or mocked
some mocked; others said, we will hear thee again of this matter.
1 Peter pictures an answer given to someone who asks
to every man that asketh you a reason of the hope that is in you.

games.q: your lab partner is fasting for her holy month and mentions it while you're both starving before lunch. you've never asked about it. what does Athens suggest first?
o: tell her how fasting works in your faith, so she knows you get it.
ask what the month means to her, and really listen.
keep it light; religion talk at school gets awkward fast.
games.why: Paul looked closely at what Athens honored before he spoke. swift to hear comes first; your own answer can wait until she asks.

practice: Bring to mind a friend whose beliefs differ from yours, or who holds none in particular. Write them one honest question about what gives them hope, and send it if it feels right.
Then sit with their name, and let whatever they might answer be theirs, without drafting a reply.

wordCard.voice: Friends of other beliefs. People you love who see the big questions differently, met by looking and listening first, and with an honest answer when they ask.

orig.note: the Greek word the King James renders 'meekness' in 1 Peter 3:15: gentleness.

carryVoice: Your line: gentleness and respect, the way Paul read their altar before he said a word. See you tomorrow.
